source: Falkenhainer (1988) Learning from physical analogies: a study in analogy and the explanation process (PhD thesis, PHINEAS) - definition of candidate inference
finding: A candidate inference is base information the mapping says could hold in the target. It must be consistent with the match substitutions and be structurally grounded: its parts must connect to the matched structure.
numbers: Formal definition: carryover CI = M(I_B), the base information I_B proposed as inferable, passed through the mapping function M. SME replaces base entities with target entities.
quote: Not just any information can be carried over - it must be consistent with the substitutions imposed by the gmap, and it must be structurally grounded
limits: Definition only. Thesis treats a gmap's candidate inferences as hypotheses, not facts.
agent_relevance: O7 should make the transferred step a hypothesis tied to matched structure, never a fact. Code can check grounding: every transferred item must touch a mapped item.

source: Falkenhainer (1988) Learning from physical analogies: a study in analogy and the explanation process (PhD thesis, PHINEAS) - skolem entities
finding: When a candidate inference mentions a base entity with no target partner, SME invents a new hypothetical target entity written as a skolem function of the base entity.
numbers: Worked case: dissolving to evaporation. Output contained (:skolem water1) because the alcohol scenario had no object matching the water. The same output also proposed (Solid alcohol1), which is false.
limits: Skolem entities and false conditions both appear in one raw output; neither is usable until repaired.
agent_relevance: O7 output has two kinds of defect to flag in code: unfilled slots (new unnamed objects) and statements that contradict known target facts. Treat both as open questions for the test step.

source: Falkenhainer (1988) Learning from physical analogies: a study in analogy and the explanation process (PhD thesis, PHINEAS) - usable versus adopted inferences
finding: Falkenhainer separates three states. Candidate inference (from mapping). Usable inference (operational: no contradiction, no unknown objects). Useful or adopted inference (tested by further problem solving and found satisfactory).
numbers: No numeric result. Candidate inferences are said to 'need not be usable' and may need 'significant adaptation'.
limits: Conceptual distinction; the thesis implements it in PHINEAS only for qualitative physics domains.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our states: a transferred step is candidate, becomes usable after a consistency check, and is adopted only after a held-out test (G3). Name these three statuses in the trace.

source: Falkenhainer (1988) Learning from physical analogies: a study in analogy and the explanation process (PhD thesis, PHINEAS) - transfer: probe and resolve phases
finding: PHINEAS repairs candidate inferences in two phases. Probe: look for alternatives in what is already derivable or assumable from target knowledge. Resolve: go beyond current knowledge, e.g. hypothesise a new object or predicate. If neither works, reject the analogy.
numbers: Probe examines each proposed fact, then each skolem object. Transfer may branch into several (mapping, inference) pairs.
limits: Repair needs a target theory rich enough to probe; with an empty target, almost everything stays a conjecture.
agent_relevance: A concrete recipe for O7 repair: check each transferred fact against the target, try to fill each unknown slot from target facts, only then invent. Rejecting the whole analogy is a legal outcome.

source: Falkenhainer (1988) Learning from physical analogies: a study in analogy and the explanation process (PhD thesis, PHINEAS) - validity problem and non-monotonic binding
finding: Falkenhainer names the validity problem: what justifies confidence in an analogically proposed inference. He lists four ways to raise validity (representation, access, mapping, verification) and notes that a candidate inference may only be an artefact of which part of the target was retrieved.
numbers: No numbers. Key claim: 'Not all candidate inferences are real inferences' because a different retrieved target description might already contain the fact.
limits: Argument from design, supported by examples rather than experiments.
agent_relevance: Before testing a transferred step, re-query the target description for it. Some surmises are already true or already false in the problem text.

source: Falkenhainer (1988) Learning from physical analogies: a study in analogy and the explanation process (PhD thesis, PHINEAS) - PHINEAS evaluation record
finding: PHINEAS was run on a handful of physics analogies. It mapped liquid flow to heat flow, dissolving to evaporation, and spring-mass oscillation to an LC circuit (position to charge, velocity to current, spring and mass to C and L).
numbers: Thesis says 'tested on over a half dozen examples'. The LC circuit case needed a hint (that the capacitor holds the restorative force) and some tailoring. Verification by planned experiments completed for only one example.
limits: Hand-built knowledge bases; tiny sample; the verification stage was the least finished part. No error-rate data.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the pipeline works on hand-built cases only. Do not claim a measured accuracy for candidate inference from it.

source: Falkenhainer (1990) Analogy in Context (draft, map-and-analyze cycle)
finding: The map-and-analyze cycle checks each candidate inference in order: is it already known (ask); is there a functional analogue already believed; if none, is it consistent (abductive-ask) so it can be assumed; else look for consistent functional analogues. If the analysis fails the analogy is rejected.
numbers: Algorithm in Table 2 of the draft; no experiment counts. Some candidate inferences 'may represent facts that are true in the target, but are not explicit'.
limits: Draft for Artificial Intelligence; examples from the literature, not human data.
agent_relevance: Gives an ordered check list for transferred steps: known, replaceable, consistent, else reject. Each check can be a code or lookup step.

source: Gentner, Brem, Ferguson, Markman, Levidow, Wolff, Forbus (1997) Analogical reasoning and conceptual change: a case study of Johannes Kepler, J. Learning Sciences 6(1):3-40 - SME projection step
finding: SME aligns base and target, then adds to the target every base predicate that belongs to the common structure but is missing from the target. These are the candidate inferences. Relations must match identically; entities may differ.
numbers: Example: ATTRACTS(Sun, planet) can map to ATTRACTS(magnet, nail) but never to COMPOSED-OF(nail, iron).
limits: Description of the model, not a test.
agent_relevance: Restricting what may transfer to items attached to the aligned structure is the built-in guard against random surmises.

source: Gentner, Brem, Ferguson, Markman, Levidow, Wolff, Forbus (1997) Analogical reasoning and conceptual change: a case study of Johannes Kepler, J. Learning Sciences 6(1):3-40 - light to vis motrix inferences
finding: Applied to Kepler's analogy between light and the moving force from the Sun, SME produced candidate inferences that resemble what Kepler appears to have inferred, for example that the vis motrix travels from the Sun to the planet and is detectable.
numbers: One case study; Figure 5 lists the inferences. Kepler held that light is instantaneous but the vis motrix takes time, so one candidate inference clashed with his existing belief about planetary motion.
quote: constraining the candidate inferences to be those connected to the aligned structure we can model an inferential process that is generative without overshooting
limits: Single historical case; match judged by the authors, not blind raters.
agent_relevance: Shows the useful failure mode: a candidate inference that conflicts with target knowledge is the trigger for rerepresentation or rejection. Conflict should route to O7 repair, not be silently dropped.

source: Gentner, Brem, Ferguson, Markman, Levidow, Wolff, Forbus (1997) Analogical reasoning and conceptual change: a case study of Johannes Kepler, J. Learning Sciences 6(1):3-40 - postmapping filters and restructuring risk
finding: The authors state that not all SME inferences will be correct; semantic and pragmatic constraints after mapping are needed. They also say large restructuring from one analogy is rare and risky.
numbers: Faraday example (citing Nersessian 1992): modelling magnetic fields on iron-filing lines gave an overly concrete, partly wrong model.
limits: The Faraday case is cited, not tested here. The Kepler paper was opened, the Nersessian source not.
agent_relevance: Cap how much of the target representation one transferred step may rewrite. Prefer several small analogies over one large one.

source: Klenk and Forbus (2009) Domain transfer via cross-domain analogy, Cognitive Systems Research - model
finding: Domain transfer via analogy (DTA) builds a mapping between worked examples of a known domain (translational kinematics) and a new one (rotational), then maps the two domain theories to get more conjectures. Candidate inferences are processed before being added; the new theory is accepted only if it solves the next problem, else it is erased and one retry is made.
numbers: Test-then-keep loop: accept if the problem is solved correctly; otherwise forget the transferred knowledge.
limits: Textbook physics with hand-encoded worked solutions; one learner model.
agent_relevance: This is nearly our O7: transfer a step, test it on a problem, keep it only if it passes. It has been built and measured.

source: Klenk and Forbus (2009) Domain transfer via cross-domain analogy, Cognitive Systems Research - results
finding: In one direction the analogy learner did better early than a baseline given the correct theory step by step.
numbers: Experiment 1: all 120 transfer attempts succeeded; 72 (60%) needed an extra retrieval. After problem 1 the baseline solved the next problem 45% of the time (ceiling 80%). Experiment 2: analogy 60% vs baseline 40% on problem 2; 90% vs 80% on problem 3; both 100% on problems 4 and 5; 180 transfer attempts, 120 (66%) successful.
limits: Few problems; the success tests are the system's own problem set; one domain pair.
agent_relevance: Transfer plus a pass-or-erase test can beat incremental teaching early, but about one third of transfers failed in experiment 2. The test step is what protects the agent.

source: Friedman, Barbella, Forbus (2012) Revising domain knowledge with cross-domain analogy, Advances in Cognitive Systems
finding: In a simulated learner with a day-night misconception, the best analogy mapping (gyros on a spit to the Earth) yielded 30 candidate inferences. Some were useful (the Earth rotates). Some were spurious (the Earth has beef and lamb as ingredients).
numbers: Six trials. Wrong correspondences made by SME: 4 (clouds block sun), 4 (sun shuts off), 2 (sun enters earth), 3 (correct model), 0 (no model); one more row is garbled in extraction. Unassisted success only for 'sun enters earth', 'correct model' and 'no model'; with user correction of mappings all six reached the correct model.
limits: Table values partly garbled in text extraction; simulated learner, not people.
agent_relevance: Wrong correspondences in the mapping produce wrong inferences (Chicago on the moon). A mapping with a known error needs a human or an external check; the agent should not trust inferences from a mapping it has not verified.

source: Markman and Gentner (1997) The effects of alignability on memory, Psychological Science 8(5):363-367
finding: After comparing two pictures, people later recalled more about the alignable differences (matched in role) than about nonalignable ones. Comparison focuses processing on the aligned structure, which is the same region where candidate inferences are generated.
numbers: Alignable cue recall m=2.35 correct; incorrect recall higher for nonalignable cues (0.64 vs 0.40); item analysis t(19)=3.79, p<.005; 10 picture triads, 36 participants.
limits: Memory for pictures, not inference; links to candidate inference only by theory.
agent_relevance: Predicts that an agent which has aligned two situations will attend to aligned items and neglect the rest. Surmises will rarely come from unaligned parts.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour (arXiv 2212.09196) - story analogies
finding: Using the Gentner et al. story set, GPT-3 chose the story with matching causal relations above chance overall, but not in the far (cross-domain) condition. Students did better. GPT-4 in an initial test did better.
numbers: GPT-3 overall binomial p=0.0005; near p=0.0039; far p=0.065 (not significant). Humans N=54: all conditions p<1e-22. Logistic regression GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003. 15 of 54 students chose the analogue on every trial.
limits: GPT-3 text-davinci-003; GPT-4 only a pilot in the supplement. Later work (Lewis and Mitchell 2025) shows order and paraphrase effects.
agent_relevance: Matching on causal structure across domains is the weak spot for a base model. The mapping step should be checked by code, not trusted from one pass.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour (arXiv 2212.09196) - Duncker radiation problem
finding: Paradigm of Gick and Holyoak (1980): GPT-3 given the target alone proposed injecting a radiation source into the tumour. Given the general-and-fortress story first, it gave the convergence solution and listed the correspondences (general to doctor, dictator to tumour, army to rays).
numbers: Qualitative, single problem plus other source stories (supplement S5.1-S5.4). With two distractor stories added, GPT-3 lost the solution; when told to consider the earlier stories it found the right story and the solution.
limits: Qualitative case, not a scored experiment. Original human data are from Gick and Holyoak (1980, 1983), not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as people: transfer of a solution needs the source to be retrieved, and a prompt to look back at earlier material rescues it. An explicit cue to compare is cheap.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour (arXiv 2212.09196) - matrices and letter strings
finding: On a new text matrix-reasoning task GPT-3 beat the human average. Its pattern of difficulty across problem types matched people's.
numbers: Digit Matrices, humans N=40: generative OR=1.88 (p=0.005); multiple choice OR=6.27 (p=2.3e-8); item-level correlation r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Letter strings: 100 problems per type, 57 students.
limits: Letter-string and matrix tasks are pattern induction, not inference about a specific target. Later challenged by counterfactual alphabets.
agent_relevance: Strong base-model pattern induction does not show it can transfer a step to a particular new case.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models, CogSci (arXiv 2402.08955)
finding: When the alphabet is permuted or replaced by symbols, humans stay accurate but GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 fall sharply. The authors argue this shows reliance on training-data similarity.
numbers: 136 Prolific participants; 7 alphabets x 10 problems x 6 transformation types = 420 problems per permutation size (n = 2, 5, 10, 20 letters reordered) plus 40 symbol problems. A counterfactual comprehension check was included.
limits: Zero-shot, simple prompt. Webb et al. (2024) reply that GPT-4 with code execution recovers.
agent_relevance: A transfer rule that works on familiar content may fail on rewritten content. Test transferred steps on a perturbed instance (G3).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2404.13070)
finding: Reply to Hodel and West and to Lewis and Mitchell. GPT-4 with a code-execution tool solved permuted-alphabet analogies at about human level; without code it did much worse. The authors say the failure is about counting positions, not analogy.
numbers: 46% (23/50) of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule versus 39% in human errors reported by Lewis and Mitchell.
limits: Authors of the original claim are the ones replying. Code execution is not how people solve it.
agent_relevance: The competing explanation: errors come from a weak sub-skill (indexing). Giving the agent a tool for the sub-skill, rather than more reasoning, may fix it.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2025) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models (arXiv 2411.14215) - story analogies
finding: On 18 far-analogy story problems, GPT-4 was more accurate when the correct story came first. Humans showed no order bias in the authors' account. Paraphrasing the correct story lowered both, GPT-4 more.
numbers: Order: GPT-4 ours 0.89 first (16/18), 0.61 second (11/18), 0.75 total (27/36); Webb et al. GPT-4 total 0.78 (292/373). Human rows are garbled in extraction. Paraphrase: GPT-4 0.86 (31/36) to 0.72 (26/36); humans 0.78 (564/720) to 0.70 (503/720).
limits: 18 stories only; the authors say the paraphrase difference may not be significant. Zero-shot simple prompt; no chain of thought.
agent_relevance: Randomise candidate order and compare answers across reorderings in code. Treat a mapping judgement that flips with order as a low-confidence one.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2025) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models (arXiv 2411.14215) - letter strings and digit matrices
finding: Digit matrices: moving the blank to a random position hurt GPT models sharply and left humans unchanged; replacing digits with symbols hurt neither. On harder letter strings both humans and models were poor, so the gap shrinks.
numbers: Human results from Prolific samples; GPT-3, 3.5 and 4. Exact per-condition figures not extracted.
limits: Mixed picture: brittleness in 3 of 4 variants only.
agent_relevance: Brittleness is specific, not general. A step transferred by the model needs a test on a changed layout, not only the original one.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis, Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models, ACL (arXiv 2305.17626)
finding: Raven's matrices were turned into text with numeric attribute names. PLMs then solved them zero-shot, rising with model size. Naming attributes with ordinal numbers beat random names and ASCII pictures. Splitting attributes into separate prompts helped small models most.
numbers: Center task: up to 77.2% for GPT-3 175B with ordinal naming vs 28.2% (quasi-image) and 51.8% (random naming); decomposition +2.8% for GPT-3; OPT-125M 22.2% to 45.6%; OPT-1.3B 47.2% to 72.0%. 2x2Grid 78.0% to 87.8%; 3x3Grid 86.4% to 93.2% with decomposition, above the human figure.
limits: Pattern completion on synthetic matrices; encoding choices were designed by the authors.
agent_relevance: How a situation is written changes accuracy by tens of points. The typed-relation rewrite step for mapping is worth testing as an independent variable.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR (arXiv 2310.01714)
finding: Analogical prompting asks the model to write K=3 relevant example problems (and optionally recall knowledge) before solving. It beat 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench tasks, with an average gain of +4%. Generated examples help larger models; retrieval of labelled examples is better for smaller models.
numbers: Average accuracy gain +4% over baselines; Codeforces Acc@1 (GPT3.5-turbo-16k) best row 15% vs 9-13% for baselines in Table 2 (row labels lost in extraction, so approximate). Models: GPT-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, PaLM 2, GPT-4.
limits: Self-generated examples, not a mapped candidate inference. Costs more tokens. Fails if the model lacks the knowledge. No structural score, no soundness check.
agent_relevance: A cheap version of O7 exists and pays on task accuracy but its cost at equal tokens is untested (G7). It generates analogues but does not map or verify; our version adds the mapping and the test.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024) Thought propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs, ICLR (arXiv 2310.03965)
finding: Thought Propagation has the model propose and solve analogous problems, then reuses their solutions or plans to correct the first answer. It improved shortest-path reasoning, creative writing and agent planning.
numbers: Reported average +12% absolute in finding optimal solutions (shortest path), +13% human preference (creative writing), +15% task completion (LLM-agent planning).
limits: Gains reported by the authors against baselines; analogues come from the same model, so errors can be correlated (G4).
agent_relevance: Supports the idea of transferring a solution step from a neighbour problem. Treat the gain as an upper bound until measured with a code check.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, J. Memory and Language 145:104676 (arXiv 2406.13803)
finding: Tasks ask the solver to map a source domain of words or strings to a target and produce the missing target item, which is a candidate inference. GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus and Llama-405B matched humans in several conditions but diverged on semantic distractors and some variations. GPT-4 failed to relate numbers across domains in some conditions.
numbers: Human and model match rates ranged about 0.4 to 0.9 across conditions; effects given as mixed-model coefficients (e.g. GPT-4 coef=-1.3669 in one condition). Exact cell values not recorded here.
limits: Match to a reference answer, not objective truth. Authors conclude LLMs offer a how-possibly not how-actually account.
agent_relevance: Directly measures producing a target-side item from a mapping. Models are decent but not human-like on distractors, so the mapping must be checked by code.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: analogical reasoning on narratives (arXiv 2310.00996)
finding: Models can find near (same-domain) analogies but fail on far analogies in zero-shot. GPT-4 scored below random on far analogies. Examples and chain of thought help, but the best model gets about halfway between random and humans.
numbers: Humans: 97.9% near, 94.1% average on far analogies. Models: 75.0% near; 39.6% average on far (below the 50% chance level). Far disanalogy up to 76.9%; one surface-mapping condition 33.9%.
limits: Binary classification on generated narratives; zero-shot prompt.
agent_relevance: Surface overlap fools the model on cross-domain cases. Do not rely on a model's own judgement of whether the source fits the target; compute alignment in code.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: deriving story-level analogies from LLMs (arXiv 2310.12874)
finding: Identifying story-level analogies is hard for LLMs. ChatGPT scored about 30% on multiple choice against over 85% for humans. Fine-tuning FlanT5-xxl on the new data matched zero-shot GPT-3.5 on analogy generation.
numbers: 24,388 story pairs from four sources (ProPara 6.9K, ROCStories 4.9K, Word-Analogy 7.5K, ConceptNet 5.0K). Annotator agreement kappa 47% (entity similarity) and 42% (relation similarity). Crowd vs expert Spearman 64.7% and 69.9%.
limits: Moderate annotator agreement means the labels are noisy.
agent_relevance: Even with ground truth for the analogy, models are far below people; the corpus can supply data to test any candidate-inference step.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1980) Analogical problem solving; (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Original finding behind the radiation problem: people rarely notice a useful analogy spontaneously but use it when given a hint. Known only through Webb et al. 2023 and Klenk and Forbus 2009 in this session.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Not opened; cited by opened papers.
agent_relevance: Backs a hint-to-compare step; exact rates must be filled in from the original.

source: Hodel and West (2023) Response: emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Tested GPT-3 on permuted alphabets and larger intervals and found poor performance. Described in Lewis and Mitchell (2024) and Webb et al. (2024).
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Part of the failed-replication record for LLM analogy claims.
